title: About the Centre
text:
The Centre for Household Finance is a research centre in the Department of Economics at Stellenbosch University. Household finance is the study of how, and how successfully, households use financial instruments to achieve their goals. We combine economic theory, knowledge of South Africa’s institutions and history, and survey and administrative data to address questions in this field: how consumer financial markets work, and which policies would make them work more efficiently and more equitably.
Our current work covers mortgage pricing, funeral insurance, and financial information and advice. The Research page describes each theme and lists our papers.

title: Centre for Household Finance
text:
We are a research group in the Department of Economics at Stellenbosch University. We study consumer financial markets in developing countries, and in South Africa in particular: how they work, and which policies would make them work more efficiently and more equitably.
We use the tools of applied microeconomics to study how households make financial decisions and what shapes the choices they make. To do this, we seek out survey and administrative data from sources in the public and private sectors.

title: Research

title: Research
text:
Research themes
Our work is organised into themes. Each output below is tagged with the theme it belongs to; use the tags to filter the list.
Mortgage pricing in South Africa. Using a unique dataset of mortgage applications, we study how banks price home loans in South Africa, how this pricing varies with borrower characteristics, and how willing households are to switch lenders.
The market for funeral insurance. Funeral insurance is one of the most widely purchased financial products in South Africa; life insurance remains far less common. Yet the two products deliver very similar benefits to households — cash in the event of a death — at different prices. Our work on this theme explores the drivers of demand for these products, the extent to which they are substitutes, and the implications for household welfare and public policy.
Financial information and advice. Households choose financial products with what they know and what they are told — by advisers, by lenders, and increasingly by the algorithms that screen their applications. Our work on this theme measures financial literacy in South Africa and how it varies across households, and studies the incentives of those who supply advice and explanations to consumers.

title: Research
text:
Papers


    
      
      
    





Financial Literacy in South Africa





working paper We examine financial literacy in South Africa using a nationally representative survey conducted in 2017 that includes standardized questions on financial literacy used in over 140 countries. South Africa follows patterns found in other countries: less educated and low-income respondents display low levels of financial literacy. Most countries have large gender gaps in financial literacy while the gender gap is absent in South Africa. The absence of an aggregate gender gap masks two offsetting patterns. Men are more financially literate than their female partners, but single women are more financially literate than single men.





2026


Lwanga Elizabeth Nanziri, Matthew Olckers







Incentives to Offer Algorithmic Recourse





working paper Algorithmic recourse promises to help applicants rejected by automated systems by explaining the changes needed to secure acceptance. What incentive do decision-makers, such as banks and employers, have to offer recourse? We study this question in a screening model in which recourse is both productive and selective: completing recourse improves an applicant’s value to the decision-maker, but applicants differ in their cost of completion. The optimal policy is a threshold rule: reject applicants with low scores, offer recourse to an intermediate range of scores, and accept applicants with high scores outright. Because the intermediate range spans the cutoff that would separate acceptance from rejection when recourse is not available, some marginal applicants gain a new path to acceptance, while others—who would have been accepted outright—must now clear a costly hurdle.





2026


Matthew Olckers, Toby Walsh
